newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, lawmakers hold foreign policy session.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, lawmakers hold foreign policy session.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and his advisers held a foreign policy brainstorming session with members of Congress on Wednesday night as Clinton pressed for Senate approval of a chemical weapons treaty.

The informal closed-door discussion took place over dinner at Blair House, an official government guest residence across Pennsylvania Avenue from the White House, and brought Clinton together with a bipartisan group of leading lawmakers.

"It is something the president has wanted to do since very early in the year, just to call together and convene a mini-retreat with the Congress to talk about a fairly broad range of our foreign policy objectives over the next four years," National Security Adviser Samuel Berger said.

Among topics talked over at the session were the pending enlargement of NATO, engagement with China, the international fight against terrorism and narcotics trafficking and efforts to expand world trade.

Berger, part of a group of administration participants that also included Vice President Al Gore, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, said the meeting was an important opportunity for Clinton and congressional leaders "to build a kind of bipartisan consensus around America's leadership in the world."

It occurred at a time when Russia is rankled at NATO plans to expand into former Soviet satellites, the Middle East peace process has stalemated and Clinton's China policy is under fire from House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich and others.
But of more immediate concern for Clinton and his team was the fate of the Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC), a treaty that would outlaw poison gas and other chemical weapons.
The accord takes effect on April 29, and the administration argues that the United States will be at a serious disadvantage if it has not ratified the pact by then.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said Clinton made telephone calls in the course of the day to about 10 senators to enlist their support. Critics say the treaty would not work and expose U.S. chemical companies to outside inspection.
Approval is "very much up in the air at this point," said Berger. "There is some strenuous opposition from some groups."
Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, is a leading critic of the accord. He declined to attend the dinner meeting.

Another topic of the high-powered skull session was if and when the Republican Congress will give Democrat Clinton so-called fast-track authority to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement linking the United States, Mexico and Canada.
The authority would give Clinton the power to conclude a trade agreement with Chile that Congress could vote for or against but would not be able to slow down with amendments.
